name: Villa Savoye
overview: Villa at 82 Rue de Villiers in Poissy, on the outskirts of Paris (English Wikipedia).

Commissioned in late summer 1928 by Pierre and Eugénie Savoye as a weekend house and built 1928 to 1931 (villa's site, English Wikipedia). The villa's site says the Savoyes returned to the provinces in May 1940.
Named for the Savoye family, the clients.
funding_verdict: Villa Savoye: mainly public: the French State, through the Centre des monuments nationaux (CMN)

press_items.title: no author named, "La difficile storia della Villa Savoye" (2017)
Santiago Pastor Vila, "The critical nature of the reconstruction of modern icons" (2025)

name: Cap Moderne (Villa E-1027 and Le Cabanon)
overview: Coastal site at Roquebrune-Cap-Martin made up of Eileen Gray's Villa E-1027, Le Corbusier's Cabanon and Camping Units, and the Étoile de Mer cabins. Tours start at a visitor centre in the Cap-Martin Roquebrune railway station, a 500 m walk from the site (press release, 2021).

Association Cap Moderne, a charity, was set up in 2014 to restore and open it. Centre des monuments nationaux (CMN) has run visits since 2 May 2018 and took full responsibility at the end of 2021 (Association Cap Moderne).
E-1027 is a code: E for Eileen, 10 for J (Jean), 2 for B (Badovici), 7 for G (Gray) (press release).
funding_verdict: Cap Moderne: mixed: public money from the State and regions, plus private sponsors and fundraising

press_items.title: Rory Stott, "The Controversy Regarding The Restoration of Eileen Gray's E-1027" (2013)
Renée Reizman, "Eileen Gray's Masterpiece in the French Riviera, No Longer Overshadowed by Le Corbusier" (2021)
Cassandra Tanti, "Historic modernist villa's restoration struggle" (2020)

name: Le Fresnoy - Studio national des arts contemporains
aliases: le fresnoy - studio national des arts contemporains tourcoing
overview: Art school and centre for producing and showing audiovisual, digital and artistic work at 22 rue du Fresnoy, Tourcoing, in the Métropole européenne de Lille (the space's website, Wikipedia).
Founded in October 1997 by Alain Fleischer (Wikipedia).

The building was a popular entertainment complex that operated from 1905 to 1984, with a cinema of 1,000 seats, a swimming pool later converted into a riding ring, a roller rink and a dance hall (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Le Fresnoy: public: Ministry of Culture and Hauts-de-France Region, with the participation of the city of Tourcoing

name: Kunsthaus Dahlem
overview: An exhibition house for post-war modernism in Germany in a historic studio building beside the Grunewald, near the Brücke Museum, in Berlin-Dahlem; its focus is sculpture, with painting, graphic works and photography, especially from 1945 to 1961 (Kunsthaus Dahlem website).

Opened in 2015 after a conversion of the studio building in 2014 and 2015; run by Atelierhaus Dahlem gGmbH, founded in 2013 as sole subsidiary of the Bernhard Heiliger Foundation; managing director Dr. Dorothea Schöne (Kunsthaus Dahlem website; imprint).

The building was put up between 1939 and 1942 to designs by Hans Freese as a 'state studio' for the sculptor Arno Breker, on a site the City of Berlin provided 'at the request of the Führer'; Breker used it briefly, for representation, and bombing damage made it hard to use by 1943 (Kunsthaus Dahlem website).
funding_verdict: Kunsthaus Dahlem: mainly public, Berlin Senate institutional funding through a foundation-owned non-profit company
wider_context: The house shows post-war art in a building made for a sculptor who, in the museum's words, visualised National Socialist ideology and from 1937 made sculptures for Albert Speer's buildings and the planned capital Germania; the museum sets out this history on its site (Kunsthaus Dahlem website).

name: Schinkel Pavillon
overview: An octagonal, fully glazed exhibition building on Oberwallstrasse in Berlin-Mitte, in the park of the Kronprinzenpalais near Unter den Linden (German Wikipedia; Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024).

The East German architect Richard Paulick built it in 1969; in GDR times it housed the restaurant Schinkelklause, and its entrance holds a cast-iron portal of about 1835 from Schinkel's Bauakademie, demolished in 1962 (German Wikipedia).

The art association Schinkel Pavillon e.V., founded in 2007, runs it as a platform for experimental contemporary sculpture, installation and media art, curated by the artist Nina Pohl (German Wikipedia; Schinkel Pavillon website).
funding_verdict: Schinkel Pavillon: run by an art association, with Berlin public money and federal project grants
wider_context: KW Institute, Künstlerhaus Bethanien, n.b.k. and nGbK warned that the Senate's cuts would set off a "domino effect"; culture senator Joe Chialo called them "very drastic and brutal" (ArtDog Istanbul, 10 December 2024).

Der Freitag (Laura Ewert, 13 December 2024) reported that the CDU-SPD Senate planned to cut about 12 per cent of the culture budget and that the Schinkel Pavillon "stellt sein Aus in Aussicht" (translated: "has raised the prospect of its end").

Berliner Zeitung (Ingeborg Ruthe, 27 November 2024; commentary, paywalled, only the opening was read) asked under the headline "Gibt es für Berlins beliebteste Kunstorte bald nur noch die halbe Ration?" (translated: "Will Berlin's favourite art venues soon get only half rations?") whether the cuts would starve such spaces.
The Pavillon depends on the Berlin culture budget these cuts target.

name: Sophiensæle
overview: A centre for independent performing arts at Sophienstraße 18 in Berlin-Mitte, with two historic halls, the Festsaal and the Hochzeitssaal, and a former canteen (Sophiensæle website).

Founded in autumn 1996 'as a theater by artists for artists' by Sasha Waltz, Jochen Sandig, Jo Fabian and Dirk Cieslak; directors were Amelie Deuflhard (2000 to 2007), Heike Albrecht (to 2010), Franziska Werner (2011 to 2023) and, from the 2023/24 season, Jens Hillje and Andrea Niederbuchner (Sophiensæle website).

The building is the former Craftsmen's Association House of 1904/05 with over 90 rooms; the first public meeting of the Spartakusbund took place there in 1918, forced labourers produced propaganda leaflets in the Festsaal in the Nazi era, and the Maxim Gorki Theater used the rooms as workshops in the GDR (Sophiensæle website).
funding_verdict: Sophiensæle: mainly public, Berlin Senate concept funding; amounts not stated on the pages read
wider_context: The Sophiensæle called for a demonstration against the planned Berlin culture cuts on 13 November 2024 at the Brandenburg Gate and backed the stage association's petition and an open letter to the Governing Mayor and the senators for finance and culture (Sophiensæle website).

name: Villa Esche
overview: Villa at Parkstraße 58 in Chemnitz, in the Helbersdorf locality (English Wikipedia, C3 site).
The textile manufacturer Herbert Esche (1874 to 1962) commissioned it from Henry van de Velde. It was built in 1902 and 1903 and extended in 1911 (English Wikipedia).
Named for the Esche family.
funding_verdict: Villa Esche: municipal: two City of Chemnitz companies and the city's museums, with named sponsors

name: Haus Ungers (Ungers Archiv für Architekturwissenschaft)
overview: Residence, office and library of the architect O.M. Ungers at Belvederestraße 60 in Köln-Müngersdorf (UAA site, German Wikipedia). It now houses the Stiftung Ungers Archiv für Architekturwissenschaft (UAA).
The house was built mainly in 1958 and 1959 for Ungers and his family, with his office and two ancillary flats (Einliegerwohnungen), and extended in 1989 and 1990 (Haus Ungers page).
Named for O.M. Ungers, who built it as his own house.
funding_verdict: Stiftung UAA: foundation-run: friends' dues and sponsors, with heritage support for the 2025 repairs

name: Museum Ludwig
overview: Museum of modern and contemporary art between Cologne Cathedral and the Rhine, in a building it shares with the Kölner Philharmonie.

Founded by a donation contract signed on 23 February 1976 by Peter and Irene Ludwig and the City of Cologne (museum website). The city undertook to build a museum for works made after 1900. It emerged from the Wallraf-Richartz Museum (Wikipedia).

Named for Peter Ludwig, a chocolate manufacturer and collector, who joined the firm Leonard Monheim, later renamed Ludwig Schokolade, and built it into one of Germany's leading chocolate businesses (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Museum Ludwig: mainly public: the City of Cologne, with the Ludwig gift and support from friends' groups
wider_context: In 1986 Peter Ludwig sat for busts by the sculptor Arno Breker, whom the Ludwig Museum Budapest describes as "Hitler's favorite sculptor". Wikipedia reports "fierce public criticism" of the commission, and the Budapest museum says the outcry in West Germany concerned Breker's past.
The connection to Museum Ludwig is that the commission was made by its founding donor.

press_items.title: Courtney Tenz, "Original or fake? Museum Ludwig puts its Russian avant-garde art to the test" (2020)
Madeleine Schwartz, "What a sham! On fakery and the Russian avant-garde" (December 2020 issue; online 16 January 2021)

name: mayhaus
overview: Model house ("Musterhaus") at Im Burgfeld 136 in the Römerstadt estate, Frankfurt. From the Römerstadt U1 stop it is about 100 m to Im Burgfeld and about 400 m more (society's directions page).

Built 1927 to 1928 as a two-storey single-family row house. The society's page names Ernst May as architect and Mietheim AG as client. Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky planned the kitchen and Leberecht Migge the garden (society's page). The atlas record also credits Carl-Hermann Rudloff. The page does not.
Named for May and called the "mayhaus".
funding_verdict: mayhaus: mixed: members and donors, with grants from the City of Frankfurt, Hesse and heritage bodies

press_items.title: Enrico Santifaller, "Dunkelgrün statt Taubenblau | Fünf Jahre Ernst-May-Gesellschaft" (Bauwelt 9, 2008)

name: Portikus
overview: Contemporary art institution at Alte Brücke 2 on the Maininsel, the island in the River Main in Frankfurt. It is part of the art academy Hochschule für Bildende Künste, the Städelschule (Portikus).
Founded in 1987 by Kasper König, who was its first director until 2001 (Portikus; English Wikipedia).
Named for a portico of a public library built in 1825 that was destroyed in the Second World War (English Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Portikus: publicly funded: the City of Frankfurt and the state of Hesse, with a non-profit foundation behind the building

name: Hohenhof (Osthaus Museum Hagen)
overview: Villa at Stirnband 10 in the Hohenhagen garden suburb of Hagen, a site of the city's Osthaus Museum and an anchor point of the Route der Industriekultur (museum site, Wikipedia).
Henry van de Velde designed it for the patron Karl Ernst Osthaus and his wife Gertrud. Osthaus commissioned it in 1906 and it was ready for occupancy in 1908 (museum site).

Van de Velde designed the furniture, wall decorations, floor coverings, lamps, fabrics, crockery and cutlery, and works by Hermann Haller, Ferdinand Hodler, Henri Matisse and Johan Thorn Prikker are built into it (museum site).
funding_verdict: Hohenhof: mainly public: the City of Hagen owns it and runs it through its Osthaus Museum, with named friends and one individual donor
wider_context: Michael Otto chaired the Otto Group's executive board from 1981 to October 2007 and its supervisory board until 1 March 2025 (English Wikipedia).

In August 2011 the broadcaster ARD showed "Das Hermes-Prinzip: Ein Milliardär und seine Götterboten", a report on wage dumping and precarious conditions among couriers of Hermes Europe, an Otto Group subsidiary. Otto and Hermes denied it and blamed individual subcontractors; in September 2011 Hermes said it had ended work with several (English Wikipedia).
The link to the space: the museum's friends page lists Dr. Michael Otto of Hamburg as a Förderer, with no amount, year or purpose.

name: GfZK, Galerie für Zeitgenössische Kunst Leipzig
overview: Museum of contemporary art at Karl-Tauchnitz-Strasse 9 to 11 in Leipzig's Music Quarter, at the edge of the Johanna Park, on the grounds of the Herfurth Villa (GfZK).

It grew from an idea of the East German art historian Klaus Werner; in November 1990 Werner and Arend Oetker, a member of the Kulturkreis der deutschen Wirtschaft im BDI, founded the Friends of the GfZK association, which still runs today (GfZK).

The villa, built from 1892 for Hermann Credner and later bought by Edgar Herfurth, was converted by Peter Kulka from 1996 to 1998 and opened in 1998; a second building by AS-IF opened in November 2004 with more than 1,000 square metres of exhibition space (GfZK).
funding_verdict: GfZK: mixed public and private: the City of Leipzig, the Free State of Saxony and the Friends of the GfZK, in equal shares in 2016

name: Weissenhofmuseum im Haus Le Corbusier
overview: Museum in Le Corbusier's double house at Rathenaustraße 1 in Stuttgart. It is the only building on the Weissenhof Estate open to visitors (museum's site).
Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret designed two semidetached houses in 1927 for the Deutscher Werkbund exhibition "Die Wohnung". The museum opened on 26 October 2006 (museum's site).
Named for the Weissenhof Estate and for Le Corbusier.
funding_verdict: Weissenhofmuseum: mainly public: City of Stuttgart grants to the association that runs it, plus tickets

name: Skulpturenpark Waldfrieden
overview: Sculpture park at Hirschstraße 12 in Wuppertal, in a wooded area in the hills above the Elberfeld and Barmen districts (EGHN); German Wikipedia puts it at 14 hectares in the Hesselnberg district of Barmen.

Founded on the private initiative of the British sculptor Tony Cragg and his wife, the artist Tatjana Valsang; Cragg bought the abandoned Waldfrieden estate in 2006 and the park opened in 2008 under the Cragg family's non-profit foundation (park's site), in September 2008 (German Wikipedia).
Named for the Villa Waldfrieden on the estate, also called "Villa Herberts", where the chemicals entrepreneur Kurt Herberts lived from the late 1940s until his death in 1989 (German Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Skulpturenpark Waldfrieden: privately funded: Tony Cragg and the Cragg family's foundation, plus tickets, tours, venue hire and donations

name: Haus Rabe
overview: House museum and exhibition venue at Ebertstraße 26 in Zwenkau, in the Landkreis Leipzig (house's site).

The Zwenkau doctors Erna and Erich Rabe commissioned it from the architect Adolf Rading, who designed it in 1929 and 1930 (L-IZ, Vielfalt der Moderne). German Wikipedia gives 1929 to 1931. Authorities first rejected the design as "undeutsch" (German Wikipedia).
Named for the Rabe family.
funding_verdict: Haus Rabe: mainly public: a district foundation that bought the house with federal money, plus ticket income and small supporters

name: Gallery 1957
overview: Commercial contemporary art gallery in Accra with three spaces: Gallery 1957 I, II and III, at the Kempinski Hotel Gold Coast City and the Galleria Mall in Ridge, plus a London space at 1 Hyde Park Gate (gallery website).
Founded by Marwan Zakhem. Opened on 6 March 2016, Ghana's Independence Day (Wikipedia). The first space was 140 square metres inside the newly built Kempinski hotel (The Art Newspaper, 2016).
Named for 1957, the year Ghana gained independence (The Art Newspaper).
funding_verdict: Gallery 1957: self-funded: its founder, Marwan Zakhem, and a commercial gallery model

name: blaxTARLINES KUMASI
overview: Artist collective, organisational network and art incubator at the Department of Painting and Sculpture, Faculty of Art, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi (KNUST); it "works in association with, yet independent from, KNUST" (e-flux, Doreen Mende, 2026).

Formally instituted in 2015 to reform the KNUST College of Art's curriculum (The State of the Arts); Brooklyn Rail describes a group of teachers and students "dissatisfied with the colonial legacy" of that curriculum.
It grew from kąrî'kạchä seid'ou's Emancipatory Art Teaching project, begun at KNUST in 2003 (The State of the Arts); e-flux names seid'ou and Edwin Bodjawah as cofounders.
funding_verdict: blaxTARLINES KUMASI: artist-run network based in a university art department, working through joint programmes with partner institutions

name: State of Concept Athens
overview: Non-profit contemporary art institution in Koukaki, Athens, at Tousa Botsari 19 (State of Concept website). Wikipedia calls it the first institution of its kind to operate in Greece.
Founded in 2013 by the art critic and curator iLiana Fokianaki, who is its founding director (State of Concept website).

The programme examines power structures, geopolitics, national identity and cultural histories from a feminist and intersectional approach, using the framework of "ministries", "departments" and "bureaus" to critique institutions (State of Concept website).
funding_verdict: State of Concept Athens: non-profit funded by grants and cultural partners: European Cultural Foundation, Outset Contemporary Art Fund (Greece), Goethe Institut Athens

press_items.title: Max L. Feldman, "a.O. - b.c.: An Audiovisual Diary at Athens School of Fine Arts and State of Concept" (7 February 2020)

name: TAVROS
overview: Non-profit art space at Anaxagora 33 (1st floor), Tavros (stated by the space), in an inner suburb of Athens, above a boxing gym (Flash Art, Ellena Savage, 22 April 2025).

Founded by locus athens, Maria-Thalia Carras and Olga Hatzidaki. It opened in October 2019 with Jonas Dahlberg's "(Of) Public Interest", on view 31 October to 27 December 2019 (e-flux, 29 October 2019). Carras co-created locus athens with Sophia Tournikiotis in 2004, and the project travelled between sites until TAVROS opened (Flash Art).
The space says Tavros is named after the Toros mountain region in Turkey, whose migrants settled in the area in the 1920s (stated by the space, translated from its text).
funding_verdict: TAVROS: independent non-profit: project funders named at the 2019 opening were a Greek ministry, a Greek foundation, the EU and Faliro House, plus donations from Friends
